title: Problem Overview
content:
**Erdős Problem #816: Equal-Degree Vertices and Paths of Length 3**

A problem of Erdős and Hajnal asking:

If G has 2n+1 vertices and n² + n + 1 edges, must it contain two vertices of the same degree connected by a path of length 3?

**Answer:** YES (Chen-Ma, 2025)

**Key Insight:** K_{n,n+1} with n² + n edges is the unique obstruction.
mathContext: This is a Turán-type extremal graph problem about forced substructures.

title: Path of Length 3 and Symmetry
content:
**hasPath3:** A path of length 3 from u to v consists of 4 distinct vertices u - a - b - v where consecutive pairs are adjacent.

**hasPath3_symm:** Constructive proof that paths of length 3 are symmetric: if there's a path from u to v, reversing gives one from v to u.

Path length 3 is crucial: in bipartite graphs, each step alternates parts, so length-3 paths between same-part vertices don't exist.
mathContext: In bipartite graphs, paths alternate between parts, so length-3 paths between same-part vertices don't exist.

title: Equal-Degree Path-3 Pair
content:
**sameDegree:** Two vertices have the same degree in graph G.

**hasEqualDegreePath3Pair:** The main property: existence of distinct vertices with same degree connected by path of length 3. This is what the problem asks whether dense graphs must have.
mathContext: See annotation content for formal details of equal-degree path-3 pair

title: Erdős-Hajnal and Chen-Ma Conditions
content:
**satisfiesEH816:** A graph has 2n+1 vertices and n² + n + 1 edges (original problem).

**satisfiesWeakerEH816:** A graph has 2n+1 vertices and at least n² + n edges (Chen-Ma's stronger version). With this weaker condition, only K_{n,n+1} fails.
mathContext: See annotation content for formal details of erdős-hajnal and chen-ma conditions

title: Complete Bipartite Graph and Counterexample
content:
**isCompleteBipartite:** K_{n,n+1} is the complete bipartite graph with parts of size n and n+1. All edges go between parts, giving n² + n total edges.

**K_counterexample:** K_{n,n+1} does NOT contain an equal-degree path-3 pair. Part A has degree n+1, part B has degree n, so same-degree vertices are in the same part. But length-3 paths between same-part vertices don't exist in bipartite graphs.

This shows the threshold n² + n + 1 is tight.
mathContext: K_{n,n+1} is the unique extremal graph for the problem.

title: Chen-Ma Theorem and Main Results
content:
**chen_ma_theorem:** For n ≥ 600, every graph on 2n+1 vertices with ≥ n² + n edges contains an equal-degree path-3 pair, EXCEPT K_{n,n+1}.

**erdos_816_for_large_n:** Corollary for n ≥ 600 with n² + n + 1 edges (G cannot be K_{n,n+1} since it has fewer edges).

**erdos_816_full:** The complete answer for all n: axiomatized as the full resolution of Problem #816.
mathContext: Chen-Ma (2025, arXiv:2503.19569) resolved this decades-old Erdős-Hajnal problem.

title: Pigeonhole for Degrees
content: **pigeonhole_degrees:** In any graph with at least 2 vertices, some pair of vertices must share a degree. There are only n possible degrees (0 to n-1) among n vertices, so by pigeonhole, at least two coincide.
mathContext: See annotation content for formal details of pigeonhole for degrees

title: Summary
content:
**erdos_816_summary:** The complete resolution: for all n, graphs with 2n+1 vertices and n² + n + 1 edges contain equal-degree vertices joined by path of length 3.

**Stronger Result:** For n ≥ 600, even n² + n edges suffice, except K_{n,n+1}.

**Threshold:** K_{n,n+1} has exactly n² + n edges and fails. One more edge forces the property.
mathContext: See annotation content for formal details of summary
